subtype: Approach: chooses a partner who is kind but firm and sets clear questions [Revision]
passage:
Subject: Would you be my Friday check-in?

Dear Kalyani,

For two months I have been checking in about my portfolio project with a friend from the design team. It was warm and I loved it, but every week ended with "no worries, next week". Nothing moved. I think I need someone who will ask straight. You are senior in our studio, and when you reviewed my slides last month you were kind and also clear about what was missing, so may I ask you? Here is my idea for the format: ten minutes on Friday, and three lines from me beforehand: what I did, what is next, what is stuck. You ask about those three, nothing else. If it stops being honest, we say so and stop. Would that work for you?

Pooja

qa.q: What three lines will Pooja send beforehand?
qa.a: Pooja will send three lines: what I did, what is next, what is stuck.

qa.q: How was Pooja feeling about the earlier weekly check-ins, and why?
qa.a: Pooja felt frustrated and stuck, since every week ended with "no worries, next week" and nothing moved.

qa.q: What could Pooja and Kalyani do if the Friday format starts to feel like a formality?
qa.a: They could change the questions or look at a piece of finished work together, so that the check-in stays honest.

qa.q: How might Kalyani feel on receiving the request?
qa.a: Kalyani may feel flattered and a little responsible, and may appreciate that the format is short and clear.

grounding: Shows a person moving to a senior colleague as a partner and proposing a short weekly format with clear questions.

subtype: Approach: drops a project that is not working after some effort [Thinking]
passage:
In the school craft room, Pradeep had been building a tall tower of ice-cream sticks for three afternoons. It kept leaning. Each time the top piece went on, the glue slipped. Pradeep held the wobbly tower and said out loud, "This glue is too slippery for so many sticks. If I add more days it will still fall."

Gurleen, the craft teacher, walked by and only asked, "What will you do?"

Pradeep took a breath. "I'll stop this one. I'll build a small hut instead, with only ten sticks, and use the strong paste from the shelf."

He put the tower gently in the box. By evening the hut stood by itself. It was small, but it did not lean.

qa.q: How many afternoons had Pradeep been building the tower?
qa.a: Pradeep had been building the tower for three afternoons.

qa.q: How was Pradeep feeling while holding the wobbly tower?
qa.a: Pradeep was frustrated and unsure, but thoughtful, saying that more days would not stop it falling.

qa.q: What could Pradeep try if the hut also leans?
qa.a: Pradeep could dry each layer before adding the next, or ask Gurleen which paste holds best.

qa.q: How might Gurleen see Pradeep's decision?
qa.a: Gurleen may feel pleased that Pradeep decided alone after being asked only one question.

grounding: Shows a boy dropping a big model when the glue will not hold and starting a smaller design instead of spending more days.

subtype: Approach: considers what has already been spent and decides based on what lies ahead [Thinking]
passage:
Lalit walked home along the canal path with Chetan after the evening class at the town institute. It was the accounts course, twice a week, and Lalit had done six months of it and disliked every session.

"Six months gone," said Chetan. "If you leave now, all that is wasted."

Lalit kicked a stone. "That's the wrong question. Those six months are gone whether I stay or not. The question is the next six." He counted on his fingers. "Six more months, Tuesdays and Saturdays, four hours each. Would I rather spend those on this, or on the drawing class that starts in June?"

He was quiet for a minute. "The drawing class. I keep what I learned about spreadsheets. I don't need the certificate."

qa.q: How many months of the course had Lalit already done?
qa.a: Lalit had done six months of the course.

qa.q: How did Lalit feel about the accounts course?
qa.a: Lalit disliked every session and was reluctant to spend more time on it.

qa.q: What could Lalit do before leaving the course?
qa.a: Lalit could talk with the institute and family, and check whether part of the course can be kept, so that the decision rests on facts about what lies ahead.

qa.q: How might Chetan see Lalit's reasoning?
qa.a: Chetan may feel surprised, having thought that leaving meant wasting the six months, and may be persuaded by the new question.

grounding: Shows a student asking whether the next six months are worth it instead of whether the first six were wasted.

subtype: Approach: sets a review point in advance to decide whether to continue [Action]
passage:
In the kasba engineering college hostel, Baljeet was starting a small app that shows bus timings for the town. Before he wrote a single line, he took a page and wrote: "Review on 15 September. If fewer than fifty people use it, I stop and spend the time on placement preparation." He pinned it above his desk and showed Suraj, his roommate. "Hold me to it."

Three months later, on the fifteenth, they opened the counter together. Nineteen users. Baljeet looked at it for a long time, then closed the laptop. "That was the deal." He felt a little heavy, but the next morning he opened the aptitude book at page one. The page above the desk stayed where it was.

qa.q: How many users did the app have on the review day?
qa.a: The app had nineteen users.

qa.q: How did Baljeet feel when he closed the laptop?
qa.a: Baljeet felt a little heavy and disappointed, but accepted it because it was the deal.

qa.q: What could Baljeet do to keep the lessons from the project?
qa.a: Baljeet could write down what he learned about users and about building the app, to use in later projects or placement interviews.

qa.q: How might Suraj see holding Baljeet to the rule?
qa.a: Suraj might feel awkward but supportive, since Baljeet asked for it and the rule was set in advance.

grounding: Shows a student setting a review point in advance and stopping the side project when the target is missed.

subtype: Approach: keeps going only because so much has been invested [Pitfall]
passage:
'Users dropped again,' Raghav said, turning the laptop around. 'Nine hundred, down from four thousand.'

'It's a dip,' said Hansa.

'Hansa, it's been two years of dips.'

'I put my savings in. The whole team's time. Two years. If we stop, all of it is gone.'

'And if you carry on?'

'Then we can fix it.'

'Fix what? Last month you told me you don't know why they leave.'

Hansa looked at the wall. 'I can't be the person who quit after two years.'

'The two years are gone either way. What matters is what the next year buys.'

'I don't have an answer,' said Hansa quietly. 'I just can't press the button.'

qa.q: How many users remained?
qa.a: Nine hundred users remained, down from four thousand.

qa.q: What is Hansa afraid of?
qa.a: Hansa is afraid of being the person who quit after two years, and feels the past effort would be wasted.

qa.q: What could Hansa do instead of carrying on?
qa.a: Hansa could set a review point with clear numbers and find out why users leave, then decide by what the next year could bring, not by what was spent.

qa.q: How might Raghav feel during this talk?
qa.a: Raghav may feel worried and frustrated but caring, trying to help Hansa look ahead.

grounding: Shows a founder continuing a failing product for two years because of what has already been invested.

subtype: Approach: stops, records the lessons and redirects the effort [Revision]
passage:
Sunday night. Today I closed the app. Turned off the servers, sent the last email to users, and hugged Ankita at the doorway. It hurt more than I expected. Then, before the feeling could settle, I opened a notebook and wrote two pages headed What I learned. About the market: people wanted a cheap, simple tool, not our long list of features. About us: we never spoke openly when the numbers dropped, and we hired before we knew the need. I underlined three lessons. Ankita is going to help with the next idea: a small tool, one feature, and a check with real users in the first month. It is smaller. It feels lighter.

Uday

qa.q: What did Uday write in the notebook?
qa.a: Uday wrote two pages headed What I learned, about the market and about the team.

qa.q: How did Uday feel about closing the app?
qa.a: Uday felt hurt, more than expected, and also a sense of lightness about the smaller plan.

qa.q: How could Uday use the lessons?
qa.a: Uday could use them to build a one-feature version with an early user check, and talk openly with Ankita when numbers drop.

qa.q: How might Ankita feel on the day the app closed?
qa.a: Ankita may feel sad about the closing but hopeful, and glad to help with the next idea.

grounding: Shows a founder closing a product, writing down what was learned about the market and the team, and redirecting effort to a smaller venture.

subtype: Approach: grabs the object first without thinking [Action]
passage: I'm Raghav, and I watched my little sister Urmila at the table. Mummy had put a red spinning top there, next to a glass of water. Urmila saw the top and her hand shot out. She did not look at the glass. Splash! Water ran over the table edge. Urmila stared at her wet sleeve and then at Mummy. I don't know if she was scared or surprised. Mummy said, "Let's wipe it together."

qa.q: What did Urmila reach for?
qa.a: Urmila reached for a red spinning top.

qa.q: What might Urmila have felt after the splash?
qa.a: Urmila may have felt surprised or startled, staring at her wet sleeve, though Raghav cannot be sure.

qa.q: What could Mummy do next time?
qa.a: Mummy could keep the glass away from the toy, so that wanting the toy does not lead to a spill.

qa.q: How might Mummy have felt about the splash?
qa.a: Mummy seemed calm, since Mummy offered to wipe it up together instead of scolding.

grounding: Shows a toddler reaching for a bright toy at once and knocking over a glass with no planning in between.

subtype: Approach: acts on the first idea and then regrets [Pitfall]
passage: Manoj looked at the photo of his cousin Rishi with a neat fringe. He wanted one too. While Mummy was in the kitchen, he found the small scissors in the drawer and snipped at his hair. Snip. It went crooked, high on one side. In the mirror his mouth began to tremble. "Mummy..." Mummy Parveen came in, took the scissors gently and put them on the high shelf. "Oh, Manoj." She hugged him. "Next time ask me first." Manoj sniffed. "I wanted to look like Rishi."

qa.q: Whose fringe did Manoj want?
qa.a: Manoj wanted a fringe like his cousin Rishi's.

qa.q: How did Manoj feel when he saw the crooked fringe?
qa.a: Manoj felt upset and sorry, shown by his trembling mouth.

qa.q: What could Manoj do next time he wants a new look?
qa.a: Manoj could ask Mummy first, so that she can take him for a proper haircut.

qa.q: How might Mummy Parveen have felt?
qa.a: Mummy Parveen might have felt worried but gentle, hugging Manoj instead of scolding.

grounding: Shows a child cutting his own fringe to look like his cousin without thinking what could go wrong, then regretting it.

subtype: Approach: learns to pause and count before acting [Revision]
passage:
Note, Class 5, week 3. Uday's hand shoots up before I finish reading a question. On Monday I asked, "What is 7 plus 8, minus 5?" and Uday called "15" at once. The answer was 10. His face fell and he looked at his desk. At break I sat with him and offered a small trick: count silently to three, then read the question again. On Wednesday he raised his hand after a long breath and answered a fraction question correctly. By Friday he glanced at the question card twice each time. I praised the checking, not the speed.

Minakshi, class teacher

qa.q: What answer did Uday call out on Monday?
qa.a: Uday called "15" at once.

qa.q: How did Uday feel after the wrong answer?
qa.a: Uday felt embarrassed and disappointed, since his face fell and he looked at his desk.

qa.q: What else could Uday do to avoid blurting out?
qa.a: Uday could jot the answer on a scrap of paper first, or wait until the teacher says a name.

qa.q: How might a classmate see Uday's new pause?
qa.a: A classmate may see Uday as more careful, and may feel there is a fair chance to answer too.

grounding: Shows a boy who blurted a wrong answer learning to count to three and re-read the question before answering.

subtype: Approach: buys something on a sudden urge [Pitfall]
passage: I'm Yogesh, and I still feel a little sick thinking about last Diwali. Relatives had given me festival money, and I had promised myself to keep some for school books and notebooks in June. Then an advertisement popped up: a tiny speaker with coloured lights, today only. My heart raced. I did not ask anyone, not even Lalit, who was with me at the shop. I bought it in ten minutes. It sounded fine for a week. When June came, the book fee and the notebooks were due and my pocket was empty. I had to ask Papa, who was tired after work and did not say much. That silence was worse than a scolding.

qa.q: What did Yogesh buy?
qa.a: Yogesh bought a tiny speaker with coloured lights.

qa.q: How did Yogesh feel when June came and the pocket was empty?
qa.a: Yogesh felt ashamed and regretful, and Papa's silence made it worse.

qa.q: What could Yogesh do next time an advertisement tempts Yogesh?
qa.a: Yogesh could wait a day and check the school needs first, or ask a trusted person before buying.

qa.q: How might Papa have felt when asked for the money?
qa.a: Papa may have felt tired, disappointed or worried, and chose silence over words.

grounding: Shows a teenager spending festival money on an advertised gadget on impulse and later lacking money for books and notebooks.
